641.quote_or_event: “Sweetness and humility, O Nanak, are the essence of virtue and goodness.”
641.explanation: In Asa ki Vaar Guru Nanak names sweetness (mithat), above all in speech and bearing, together with humility as the very essence of every virtue.
641.tie_back: The Kural calls goodness of the tongue a wealth in its own right, not one good among many; Guru Nanak likewise sets sweetness at the core of all goodness rather than treating it as a minor accomplishment.
641.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 470, Raag Aasaa (Asa ki Vaar, salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
641._accuracy_note: Strong thematic fit on the supreme value of sweet speech, though Guru Nanak pairs it with humility as a spiritual virtue, while the Kural treats eloquence as a minister's asset.

642.quote_or_event: “Those words are acceptable, which, when spoken, bring honor. Harsh words bring only grief. Listen, O foolish and ignorant mind!”
642.explanation: Guru Nanak teaches that speech is the hinge of a person's standing: words that bring honour are accepted, while harsh or insipid words bring only ruin and grief.
642.tie_back: The Kural says both prosperity and ruin come through speech, so one must guard against any slip of the tongue; Guru Nanak names the same two outcomes, honour and grief, as the fruit of what one says.
642.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 15, Siree Raag, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
642._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one: both texts make speech the source of either honour or ruin; Gurbani adds that the honour that counts is acceptance in God's court.

643.explanation: In the Suniai (Listening) stanzas of Japji, Guru Nanak praises the transforming power of hearing the divine Word, which holds and changes those who attend to it.
643.tie_back: The Kural praises speech that binds its hearers and makes others long to hear it; Japji's refrain shows the Sikh sense of a Word so powerful that hearing it alone transforms the listener.
643.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 2, Jap (Japji Sahib, Pauri 8), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
643._accuracy_note: Next-best only: Japji praises the power of hearing God's Name, not human eloquence, so the parallel lies only in the compelling force of a word on its listeners.

644.quote_or_event: At Hardwar, according to the Janamsakhi tradition retold by Macauliffe, Guru Nanak saw pilgrims throwing water eastward to their ancestors and began throwing water westward himself. When the gathered crowd asked why, he said he was watering his fields in the Punjab; when they laughed that it could never reach so far, he asked how their water could then reach ancestors far beyond.
644.explanation: Rather than lecture the pilgrims, the Guru staged a gesture suited to his audience that drew a crowd and let them reach the lesson through their own objection.
644.tie_back: The Kural tells the speaker to know the nature of his hearers before speaking, since nothing is more effective than words fitted to them; the Hardwar episode shows Guru Nanak choosing a form of teaching exactly matched to his listeners.
644.source: Max Arthur Macauliffe, The Sikh Religion, vol. 1 (1909), Life of Guru Nanak, ch. IV, pp. 50-51
644._accuracy_note: Reasonable but partial: a hagiographic (Janamsakhi) account that illustrates audience-fitted teaching by action as much as by speech; the Kural's point concerns spoken counsel.

645.quote_or_event: At Gorakhmata, Macauliffe relates from the Sikh biographies, Siddhs pressed the young Guru Nanak to put on the yogi's dress; he answered with a hymn saying religion lies not in patched coats, earrings or ashes but in living pure amid the impurities of the world, and the Siddhs, unable to answer him, made obeisance.
645.explanation: Guru Nanak met the yogis on their own ground with a reply so complete that it ended the dispute, a pattern repeated in his recorded discourses with the Siddhs.
645.tie_back: The Kural advises speaking only after making sure no other word can defeat yours; in this account Guru Nanak's answer to the Siddhs left them no rejoinder.
645.source: Max Arthur Macauliffe, The Sikh Religion, vol. 1 (1909), Life of Guru Nanak, ch. V, pp. 59-61
645._accuracy_note: Reasonable but partial: a hagiographic account of a debate won by an unanswerable reply; the Kural's verse is about verbal craft in general, not religious debate.

646.quote_or_event: “One who has a basket of fragrant virtues, should enjoy its fragrance. If my friends have virtues, I will share in them.”
646.explanation: Guru Nanak urges drawing out the fragrance of virtue wherever it is found and sharing in the good qualities of one's companions.
646.tie_back: The Kural praises those who speak so others long to hear and who take the useful meaning from others' words; Guru Nanak likewise asks us to take in the good that others hold.
646.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 765, Raag Soohee, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
646._accuracy_note: Reasonable but partial: matches the second half (taking the good from others) but concerns sharing virtues, not listening to speech, and leaves out the speaking half.

647.quote_or_event: “Nanak speaks the Word of Truth; he proclaims the Truth at this, the right time.”
647.explanation: This line closes Guru Nanak's hymn in Tilang on Babur's invasion, in which he openly condemned the violence of the conquest while it was happening.
647.tie_back: The Kural says no one can overcome a speaker who is forceful, never slips, and does not fear; Guru Nanak's fearless proclamation of truth to power shows that kind of unshaken speaker.
647.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 723, Raag Tilang, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
647._accuracy_note: Strong thematic fit on fearless, truthful speech at the decisive moment, though the Kural is about winning in debate and the hymn is prophetic witness, not contest.

648.quote_or_event: “Humility is the word, forgiveness is the virtue, and sweet speech is the magic mantra. Wear these three robes, O sister, and you will captivate your Husband Lord.”
648.explanation: Sheikh Farid, whose saloks are included in the Guru Granth Sahib, calls sweet speech a magic mantra that, with humility and forgiveness, wins over even the divine Beloved.
648.tie_back: The Kural says that if the world finds those who speak in good order and pleasantly, it will quickly do their bidding; Farid likewise makes sweet speech the spell that brings the one addressed under the speaker's sway.
648.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1384, Salok Sheikh Farid, Salok 127 (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
648._accuracy_note: Strong fit on the persuasive power of sweet speech; Farid (a Sufi bhagat in the SGGS) speaks of winning the divine Lord, not the world, and adds nothing on ordered arrangement.

649.quote_or_event: “To speak too much and babble is useless.”
649.explanation: Guru Nanak dismisses much talking as empty babble, since God knows everything without being told.
649.tie_back: The Kural says those who cannot speak a few flawless words are the very ones who love to speak many; Guru Nanak likewise rejects wordiness as worthless.
649.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 661, Raag Dhanaasree, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
649._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one on the futility of many words; the Kural also prizes the few faultless words, which this line leaves implicit.

650.quote_or_event: “Contemplate and reflect upon knowledge, and you will become a benefactor to others.”
650.explanation: Guru Nanak teaches that learning proves itself only when, through reflection, it becomes a benefit to others.
650.tie_back: The Kural compares those who cannot make their learning understood by others to flowers that bloom without fragrance; Guru Nanak likewise judges knowledge by whether it reaches and helps others.
650.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 356, Raag Aasaa, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
650._accuracy_note: Reasonable fit on learning that must reach others to be of worth; the Kural stresses explaining clearly, while Guru Nanak stresses reflection leading to service.
